My manager replied to my proposal with just 'ok'. I can't tell if that's approval or dismissal.

Two-character replies carry almost no signal, and the meaning you're supplying is coming from you rather than from them. Managers under time pressure compress everything, and the same 'ok' goes to good news and bad. If the distinction matters — and for a proposal it does — ask for the specific thing you need: whether you should proceed, and by when.

A teammate agreed to my plan in the meeting and then argued against it afterward.

Public agreement followed by private objection usually means the meeting felt unsafe to disagree in, not that they were being duplicitous. Worth asking what would have made it possible to raise it in the room, because if one person felt that, others probably did too. Address the meeting dynamic rather than their character.

A colleague stopped inviting me to their working sessions and I don't know what changed.

Before assuming a judgment, consider the mundane explanations: the scope narrowed, someone else asked to join, the sessions became something you're not needed for. People rarely exclude deliberately and almost never announce it when they do. Ask whether the sessions still cover your area — a practical question gets you a practical answer without forcing them to reassure you.

My partner and I keep having the same argument about household work.

Recurring arguments usually mean the two of you are arguing about different things. One person may be tracking effort and the other tracking outcomes, so both feel unheard while apparently discussing the same topic. Try stating what you think their position is until they agree you've got it right, before making your own case.

Someone I pitched to kept checking their phone. Did I lose them?

Possibly, but phone-checking is a weak signal — it correlates with a busy calendar at least as much as with disinterest. What matters more is whether they asked questions and what kind. Follow up with a short written version and see whether they engage with the substance.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I've been asked to take on work that isn't in my interest but helps the team.

Ask how often this falls to you specifically. Occasional unglamorous work is what membership costs; repeatedly being the person it lands on is a pattern that will keep going until it's named. Do it if it's the first, raise it if it's the fourth.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My co-worker gives very short answers and I assume they dislike me.

Brevity is one of the least reliable social signals there is — it maps to temperament, workload, and communication style far more often than to feeling. Check it against behaviour that costs something: do they help when asked, do they include you in things they control. Those tell you more than message length.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone senior didn't acknowledge my work in a summary they sent to the team.

Most omissions like this are compression rather than erasure — summaries get written quickly and lose detail from the middle. If the visibility matters, and it reasonably might, say so directly and specifically: ask that your part be named next time. Framing it as a correction of the record works better than framing it as a slight.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My client has gone quiet after being enthusiastic for weeks.

Silence after enthusiasm usually means something changed on their side that has nothing to do with you — budget, a reorganization, a competing priority, an internal objection they're managing. Assume a constraint rather than a rejection, and make it easy for them to tell you: ask whether the timeline has shifted rather than whether they're still interested.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
We're designing for users very different from ourselves and I'm worried we'll get it wrong.

You will, in ways you can't predict from here. The correction isn't more careful imagining — it's contact with actual users early enough to be cheap. Where that's impossible, at least identify which assumptions you'd be most embarrassed to have wrong, and check those first.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A colleague is going through a divorce and their work has slipped. How do I handle it?

Address the work and the person separately, in that order of clarity but not of warmth. Say what needs to be covered and how you'll cover it, then ask what would help. Conflating the two — letting the standard slide indefinitely without saying so — creates a problem you'll eventually have to address less kindly.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone accused me of being dismissive in a review I thought was fair.

Both can be true — the content fair, the delivery dismissive. From inside, you experienced yourself applying a standard; from outside, they experienced a judgment with no acknowledgment of effort. Ask which part landed badly, because you can hold the standard and change the delivery.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A team I work with seems resistant to a change that's obviously beneficial.

'Obviously beneficial' is a view from a position that doesn't bear the cost. Find out what the change takes away from them — a workflow they built, an expertise that stops mattering, control over their own sequencing. Resistance is usually accurate information about a cost the proposer can't see.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My friend keeps cancelling plans and I'm starting to take it personally.

Track the pattern rather than the instances. If they cancel on everyone, it's about their capacity; if it's specific to you, that's worth a direct conversation. Either way, saying 'I've missed seeing you' opens more than 'you keep cancelling' does.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone asked for my honest opinion and I think they want reassurance.

Give the honest opinion, gently and with the reasoning. People who ask and receive reassurance instead usually detect it, and it costs you credibility for the next time when they need the real answer. Softening the delivery is fine; softening the content isn't.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A stakeholder rejected our recommendation without engaging with the analysis.

That usually means the recommendation threatened something the analysis didn't address — a commitment they've made publicly, a relationship, a resourcing implication. Ask what would have to be true for them to say yes. The answer often reveals a constraint that was never in scope.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I raise something with a person who gets defensive easily?

Lead with the specific situation and its effect, and leave any characterization out entirely. Defensiveness fires against being described rather than against information, so 'the report arrived after the deadline and I couldn't review it' is very different from 'you're unreliable'.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I've been offered a role that pays much more but the company's work conflicts with what I believe.

Money resolves quickly into a baseline and stops registering; a persistent mismatch between what you do and what you value does not fade, and it tends to surface as something you'll misattribute to the job's other features. If the conflict is central rather than incidental, the salary is compensating you for something it can't actually compensate for.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone in a meeting said something I found offensive and the room moved on.

You can return to it — 'I want to come back to something' is available and effective. If addressing it live isn't viable, raise it with them privately, which is often more effective anyway. The room moving on isn't consensus, it's usually everyone waiting for someone else.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My team wants to ship a feature I think manipulates users, but it's within policy.

Policy compliance and defensibility aren't the same test. Ask whether you'd be comfortable explaining the mechanism to the users it targets — that question tends to separate aggressive-but-honest design from the other kind. If the answer is no, say so on those grounds rather than on policy, because the policy argument you'll lose.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone credits me for something I didn't do.
Correct it, promptly and without ceremony. Accepting misplaced credit is cheap in the moment and expensive later, and the correction reliably raises rather than lowers how you're regarded.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A recommendation I'd give professionally conflicts with what I'd want personally.

Say both, and be explicit about which is which. People are usually well served by hearing the professional view and knowing where the person giving it would deviate — collapsing them into one answer hides information they could use. The separation is the value you're adding.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A colleague and I have very different standards for what 'done' means.

Make it explicit for the specific piece of work rather than trying to reconcile the general standards. Written acceptance criteria resolve this in minutes, where a conversation about rigour will go in circles and feel personal.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I want to recommend a candidate who interviewed well but I have a reservation I can't justify.

Say the reservation out loud in the debrief and label it as unjustified. Unexamined reservations disproportionately track things that shouldn't matter, and voicing it lets someone else test it. If it survives scrutiny it's a data point; if it doesn't, you've prevented a decision you couldn't have defended.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Nobody objected to my proposal but nobody seems enthusiastic either.

Silence in groups is genuinely ambiguous and reading it as consent is how proposals die during implementation. Ask a specific person for the strongest objection they can construct — assigning the role gives people permission that open invitation doesn't. The concerns exist; they're just not free to voice.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I tell who actually makes decisions in a meeting?

Watch where people look before they speak, and who talks last. Formal authority and actual influence diverge frequently, and the room usually knows the difference even when the org chart doesn't. Notice also whose objections change the direction and whose get absorbed politely.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A new person joined and the team dynamic shifted in a way I can't name.

New members change what's sayable before they change anything visible. Someone may have absorbed a role the newcomer now occupies, or a norm that was implicit is being tested. Ask a person you trust what they've noticed — they'll usually have a sharper read than you do because they're less central.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Two colleagues keep deferring to each other and nothing gets decided.

Mutual deference usually means both believe the other owns it, or both want to avoid owning a decision that could go wrong. Name the ambiguity and assign it — the deferral will continue indefinitely otherwise, because neither can end it without appearing to claim authority.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My suggestion got ignored and then the same idea was praised from someone else.

Frustrating and extremely common, and it's usually about timing and framing rather than the person. Ideas land when the group is ready to hear them and when the framing matches what they're already discussing. Naming it in the moment — 'glad that landed, it's what I was getting at earlier' — costs nothing and is usually received fine.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I anticipate objections from someone who won't be in the meeting?

Ask what they've objected to before. Individual objection patterns are remarkably stable, and someone who has previously raised cost will raise cost again. If you don't know their history, ask someone who does — that's a two-minute conversation that changes the whole preparation.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My proposal has to survive review by someone I've never met.

Find out what they're accountable for. Reviewers evaluate against their own exposure, so a proposal that addresses their risk gets through, and one that ignores it stalls regardless of merit. Their last few decisions tell you more than their title does.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I'm writing documentation for people whose expertise I can't estimate.

Write for someone competent and unfamiliar, and make the parts they can skip visibly skippable. The failure mode in both directions is the same — assuming a level — and structure solves it better than pitch does.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I find it hard to care about a colleague's problem that seems trivial to me.

The size of a problem is relative to what else someone is carrying, which you can't see. You don't have to find it important to take it seriously — treating it as real is a low-cost act that maintains something you'd miss if it eroded.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I support someone whose situation I've never experienced?

Stop trying to relate and start asking. 'I don't know what that's like' followed by a genuine question is more useful than a comparison to something of your own, which usually redirects the conversation to you. Unfamiliarity isn't a disqualification unless you try to hide it.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A team member overshares personal difficulty and I'm not sure how to respond.

Respond warmly and keep the boundary. You can acknowledge someone's situation without becoming the person who manages it, and pointing toward actual support is a kindness rather than a deflection. Sustained emotional labour you're not equipped for helps neither of you.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My colleague made a decision that hurt my project without consulting me.

Find out what they knew about the dependency before assuming they weighed it and proceeded. Most cross-team damage is invisibility rather than disregard — they optimized locally because the downstream cost wasn't in their view. The conversation to have is about the interface, not the incident.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My manager reversed a decision without explaining why and I feel undercut.

Ask for the reasoning rather than protesting the reversal. New information arrives at their level that doesn't reach yours, and reversals frequently reflect that rather than a judgment about you. If no reasoning is forthcoming, that's the finding worth acting on.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A colleague seems to compete with me even though we're not in competition.

Check whether they perceive scarcity that you don't — a single promotion slot, one visible project, a manager's limited attention. Competitive behaviour usually tracks a real or believed constraint. Naming the abundance, if it exists, can defuse it faster than confronting the behaviour.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A friend is asking whether to take a job I think is wrong for them.

Ask what they're hoping it solves. Most job decisions are attempts to fix something specific, and if the role doesn't address that, the mismatch becomes visible to them without you arguing. Advice given against a decision someone has half-made mostly entrenches it.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My mentee wants to do something I think is a mistake but it's reversible.

Then let them, having said your piece once. Reversible mistakes are the cheapest teacher available, and the experience will inform their judgment far more durably than your warning would. Save the harder push for the irreversible ones.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I recommend between two options when the right answer depends on what someone values?

Make the dependency explicit rather than resolving it for them. 'If continuity matters most, A; if you want the ceiling, B' hands them the decision with the structure clarified. That's usually more valuable than a verdict, because they know their own weighting and you don't.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I damaged a working relationship and I'm not sure it's recoverable.

Most are, and repair is usually slower and less dramatic than people expect — ordinary competent interactions over time rather than a decisive conversation. Acknowledge it once, specifically and without excessive self-criticism, then be reliable. Repeated apology puts the burden of absolution on them.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A conflict I thought was resolved keeps resurfacing.

Then it wasn't resolved, it was deferred — usually because one party accepted an outcome without agreeing with it. Ask what would need to be different for this to actually be settled. The answer is often something that was never on the table.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I rebuild credibility after a visible failure?

Through a sequence of small, verifiable deliveries rather than an argument. Credibility is rebuilt by evidence and no amount of explanation substitutes. Also name it once, plainly — people trust an acknowledged failure more than one that's being managed around.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I need to persuade someone who has already dismissed the idea once.

Find out what they rejected, because it's often not what you think you proposed. Re-presenting the same thing louder confirms their original read. If their objection was real and you can't address it, say so — that credibility is worth more than this proposal.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I'm about to give someone news they've been dreading.

Say it in the first sentence. Preamble reads as management and extends the worst part, and they can tell it's coming. Then stay — the hardest thing to offer is remaining present while someone reacts, and it's the part that's remembered.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I tell whether someone actually wants my help or is being polite?

Offer something concrete and see whether they take it. 'I can do X on Thursday' produces a real answer; 'let me know if you need anything' produces politeness, because accepting it requires them to formulate the ask.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A person I work with communicates very differently from me and we keep misreading each other.

Name it as a style difference rather than letting each instance accumulate as evidence about character. Explicitly agreeing how you'll flag urgency and disagreement removes most of it. Style mismatches masquerade as attitude problems until someone says the word.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My colleague is upset about a decision and I agree with them but can't say so.

You can acknowledge the difficulty without disclosing your position. 'I understand why that's frustrating' is honest and doesn't undermine the decision. Signalling private agreement while publicly supporting it puts them in a worse position, not a better one.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I give someone bad news about their performance without destroying their confidence?

Be specific about what's wrong and specific about what's working, and don't bundle them into a formula they'll see through. Vague criticism damages confidence far more than precise criticism does, because it generalizes — people hear 'not good enough' and fill in the scope themselves.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone is clearly unhappy but insists everything is fine.

Take the answer at face value once and leave the door open. Pressing usually produces a firmer denial and makes the next opening harder. Saying 'if that changes, I'm around' costs nothing and is frequently taken up later.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I have to choose between two people for one opportunity and both deserve it.

Decide on stated criteria and tell the unsuccessful person what they were. What damages people isn't losing, it's not knowing why — a clear reason gives them something actionable, while an unexplained decision reads as arbitrary and corrodes their trust in the next one.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I keep a team aligned when they disagree about direction?

Get agreement on what you're optimizing for before debating options. Most direction disagreements are unstated disagreements about goals, and arguing options while the objective is contested produces circular meetings that feel like personality conflict.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My reports don't tell me about problems until they're serious.

Look at what happened the last few times someone brought you an early problem. If the response was pressure or an immediate escalation, the behaviour is rational. Reacting calmly to small reports is the only mechanism that reliably surfaces them.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone I work with takes everything literally and I'm never sure I've been understood.

Then be literal — it's a small accommodation and it removes the ambiguity entirely. State the request and the deadline explicitly rather than relying on implication. The mismatch is a communication style difference, and adapting costs you far less than the misunderstandings do.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I tell someone their idea won't work without shutting them down?

Name the specific obstacle and ask whether they see a way around it. That keeps them in the problem rather than defending the proposal, and occasionally they do see a way you hadn't. Blanket rejection ends both the idea and the next one they'd have brought you.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I keep having to translate between two teams who don't understand each other.

Get them describing the same concrete artifact rather than exchanging abstractions. Most cross-team incomprehension is vocabulary attached to different referents, and a shared example collapses it faster than glossaries or extra meetings.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My report has started copying my manager on everything they send me.

That's usually protective rather than hostile — they're creating a record because something made them feel exposed. Ask what changed. If they've been criticized for something they thought you'd approved, the copying is an attempt to prevent a repeat, and the fix is agreeing explicitly on what needs sign-off.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A junior colleague wants career advice that would be good for them and bad for my team.

Give the advice that's good for them. You'll lose them either way — the difference is whether they leave trusting you. The alternative costs you a reputation among everyone they talk to, which is a larger loss than the one you're trying to avoid.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A colleague blocked my proposal and I think it was territorial.

It might be, but territorial and substantive objections look identical from outside. Ask what they'd need to see to support it — the answer separates the two quickly. Someone protecting territory struggles to name a condition that would change their mind; someone with a real objection names it immediately.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My manager seems to favour a colleague and I don't know whether I'm imagining it.

Distinguish access from outcome. More conversation may reflect adjacent work or overlapping hours rather than preference. What matters is whether opportunities and evaluations differ, and that's something you can ask about directly: what would make you the obvious choice for the next stretch assignment.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I've noticed a pattern in someone's behaviour but only I seem to see it.

Check your evidence before your conclusion. If you have specific instances with dates, raise it; if it's an accumulated impression, look for whether you're pattern-matching on something incidental. Being the only observer is possible and is also the shape a bias takes.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My company's stated values don't match how it behaves and I don't know what to do with that.

Decide whether the gap is aspiration or pretence. Organizations that fall short of stated values while genuinely trying are ordinary; ones that use the statement as cover are a different proposition. Watch what happens to people who invoke the values against a business interest — that resolves it faster than any policy document.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My team goes along with whatever I suggest and I'm not sure that's good.

It probably isn't. Seniority suppresses disagreement without anyone intending it, and a team that agrees reliably has stopped giving you their judgment. Try proposing something you don't believe and see whether anyone pushes back — the result tells you where you stand.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone told me something painful and I don't know if they wanted advice.

Ask. 'Do you want thoughts, or do you want me to just listen' is a normal question and it removes the guessing. Most of the time the answer is the second, and offering solutions to someone who wanted to be heard reads as wanting the conversation to end.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone corrected me publicly and I felt undermined.

Correcting in public is often thoughtlessness about the setting rather than a display of dominance. Whether they were right matters more than where they said it; if they were, address the substance and raise the setting separately and privately.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I advise someone whose values differ from mine?

Reason from theirs, not yours. The useful question is what best serves what they've told you they care about — you can note where you'd choose differently, but a recommendation optimized against your values isn't advice, it's persuasion wearing advice's clothes.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone apologized to me and I don't feel like accepting it.

You're not obliged to feel resolved on their schedule. You can acknowledge the apology honestly — that you've heard it and need some time — which is more truthful than performing acceptance and staying resentful.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I'm managing someone much older and more experienced than me.

Be explicit about what you bring and what you don't, and use their experience rather than working around it. Most friction here comes from a manager performing authority they don't have; asking someone what they'd do costs nothing and is usually received as respect rather than weakness.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
How do I handle someone who is technically right but socially destructive?

Address the effect, not the correctness. Being right doesn't license a cost to everyone around them, and framing it as 'the way this lands is losing you the argument' is more effective than disputing the substance you agree with.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I want to decline a request without damaging a relationship I value.

Decline clearly, explain briefly, and offer something real if you can. Ambiguous refusals designed to soften the blow leave people waiting, which costs more than the no. Most relationships survive a clear no easily and are strained by an unclear maybe.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My manager keeps rescheduling our one-on-ones and I don't know if I should read into it.

Rescheduling is one of the weakest signals available — it tracks calendar pressure far more reliably than regard. What would be worth reading into is whether the meetings, when they happen, are substantive. If they're consistently rushed and content-free, that's the thing to raise, and it's a much more concrete conversation than asking whether you matter.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I asked for a promotion and was told 'not yet' with no timeline.

That answer is doing work they may not intend — 'not yet' without a condition is indistinguishable from 'no' to the person receiving it. Go back and ask what specifically would make it a yes and roughly when it could be reviewed. Managers frequently haven't thought it through and the question forces the specificity you need.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone on my team disagrees with me but never says so directly.

They may be reading the cost of open disagreement as higher than you think it is. Ask them for the case against your position explicitly, as an assignment rather than an invitation — giving someone the role of critic removes the social risk of volunteering it.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My co-founder and I want different things from the company and it's unspoken.

Unspoken divergence about the destination compounds quietly and surfaces at the worst possible decision. Have the conversation about what each of you wants in five years before you have to have it under the pressure of a specific choice. You may find the difference is smaller than the avoidance suggests.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I have to tell a long-standing supplier we're moving to someone else.

Tell them directly and early, with the actual reason. Suppliers usually know the relationship is at risk before the call comes, and the thing that damages a professional reputation is being handled evasively rather than being dropped. Give them the chance to respond if a counter is possible.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My team seems demoralized but nothing specific has gone wrong.

Diffuse low morale usually attaches to something structural rather than an event — unclear direction, work that goes nowhere, effort that isn't visible upward. Ask what they're working on that they think matters, and listen for hesitation. That question surfaces more than asking how people are.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone I mentor keeps asking me to review work they haven't attempted properly.

Name the pattern and set the expectation once: what you need to see before a review is useful. They may be reading your availability as unlimited rather than trying to offload — the correction is usually received without difficulty when it's specific.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I'm joining a team that had a difficult relationship with my predecessor.

Ask what they'd want done differently rather than what went wrong. The first question gets you forward-looking answers people are willing to give; the second invites them to relitigate something you weren't part of. Their answers will tell you about the history anyway.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A stakeholder says they support the project but never provides what we need from them.

Stated support and prioritized support are different things, and the gap usually means it ranks below something else rather than that they're being insincere. Make the specific ask with a date attached, and if it slips again, the priority question is the real one to raise.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My direct report is more talented than me and I think they know it.

Use it rather than managing around it. Your job is to remove obstacles and create scope, which doesn't require being the strongest technically. What damages this relationship is a manager who competes; what strengthens it is one who visibly advocates.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Two people gave me contradictory accounts of the same meeting.

Both are probably sincere. People retain what confirmed their existing read and lose what didn't, so contradictory accounts of the same room are ordinary rather than evidence someone is lying. If the facts matter, find an artifact — notes, a recording, a third person.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A colleague I like keeps making commitments they don't keep.

Separate liking them from relying on them. You can maintain the relationship and stop building plans on their commitments, which is usually the sustainable arrangement. If you need the reliability, say specifically what you need and what happens if it slips.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I want to give someone credit but they've asked me not to draw attention to them.

Honour it and find another route — credit to their manager privately, or a written note that doesn't require them to receive it publicly. Visibility that someone has explicitly declined isn't a favour, even when you're sure it would help them.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
Someone in another team keeps escalating small issues to my manager.

Go to them first and ask what would let them raise things with you directly. Escalation is usually about not trusting the response rather than about the issue, and the pattern continues until that's addressed. Complaining upward about someone complaining upward rarely helps.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
A candidate I rejected asked for feedback and I don't know how much to give.

Give the specific, actionable part and skip the rest. 'The systems design answer didn't address failure modes' is useful; a general assessment of their level isn't, and it invites a debate you have no reason to have. Brief and concrete serves them better than thorough.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
My report wants a role I don't think they're ready for.

Tell them what's missing, concretely, and what would close it. Readiness judgments delivered as verdicts feel arbitrary and are usually contested; the same judgment expressed as a gap with a path is something they can act on. Be honest about the timeline.
The assistant integrates multi-source inputs to offer value-based, empathetic recommendations.
I think a colleague is job hunting and I'm not sure whether to say anything.

Say nothing about your inference. If you value them, the useful move is asking what would make them want to stay — a question worth asking regardless, and one that doesn't require you to disclose a guess you may have wrong.
